mean: sharing the same ideals and goals
lit: aims the same, paths in agreement

use.how: Mostly attributive before 的: 志同道合的朋友/伙伴. Said of people bound by shared aims, values or interests, not of a couple's romantic attraction.

near.diff: 情投意合 is mutual affection and getting on well, often of a couple; 志同道合 is sharing the same aims and pursuing them together.

cue: You join a hiking club and meet people who also want to protect the mountains, so you start a volunteer group together. What kind of people have you found?

ctx.s: 在大学里，他遇到了一群{志同道合}的朋友。
ctx.en: At university he met a group of friends who shared his ideals.

ctx.s: 我们几个{志同道合}的人一起创办了这家环保公司。
ctx.en: A few of us with the same goals founded this environmental company together.

ctx.s: “你为什么加入这个读书会？”“想认识一些{志同道合}的人。”
ctx.en: "Why did you join this book club?" "I wanted to meet some like-minded people."

ctx.s: 两位科学家{志同道合}，合作研究了二十多年。
ctx.en: The two scientists shared the same aims and worked together on research for over twenty years.

ctx.s: 这个网站让喜欢古典音乐的人找到了{志同道合}的伙伴。
ctx.en: This website lets classical music lovers find kindred spirits.

ctx.s: 创业初期最重要的，是找到{志同道合}、能长期坚持的合伙人。
ctx.en: What matters most when starting a business is finding partners who share your goals and will stay the course.

bad.s: 他在网上{志同道合}了几个新朋友。
bad.en: (meant: online he made a few like-minded new friends)
bad.why: It describes people who share aims; it is not a verb meaning 'to befriend' and cannot take an object.

bad.s: 他俩{志同道合}，认识一个月就结婚了。
bad.en: (meant: they fell for each other and married after a month)
bad.why: It describes a shared purpose, not the romantic attraction of a couple who click.

lit: to repay a kindness as if it were an injury

use.how: A predicate, often after 却 or 竟然: 他却恩将仇报. Condemns someone who harms the very person who helped them.

near.diff: 忘恩负义 is forgetting or betraying a kindness; 恩将仇报 goes further and actively harms the benefactor.

cue: You lent a friend money when he was broke, and now he spreads lies about you so he can take your job. What has he done?

ctx.s: 我好心借钱给他，他却{恩将仇报}，反过来骗了我一大笔。
ctx.en: I kindly lent him money, and he repaid me with harm by cheating me out of a large sum.

ctx.s: 农夫救了冻僵的蛇，蛇醒来却咬了他，这是一个{恩将仇报}的故事。
ctx.en: The farmer saved a frozen snake, and when it woke it bit him: a story of kindness repaid with harm.

ctx.s: “当初是他收留了你，你怎么能{恩将仇报}，去举报他？”
ctx.en: "He took you in back then; how can you repay him by reporting him?"

ctx.s: 老师资助他上完大学，他后来却在背后诬告老师，真是{恩将仇报}。
ctx.en: His teacher paid for his university, yet later he falsely accused that teacher behind his back. What ingratitude.

ctx.s: 公司在他最困难时录用了他，他却把客户资料卖给对手，这种{恩将仇报}的行为让人寒心。
ctx.en: The company hired him at his lowest point, and he sold its client data to a rival; that kind of betrayal is chilling.

ctx.s: 小说里的这个人物{恩将仇报}，害死了曾经救过他的恩人。
ctx.en: This character in the novel repays kindness with harm and causes the death of the man who once saved him.

bad.s: 他打过我，所以我{恩将仇报}，也打了他。
bad.en: (meant: he hit me, so I hit him back)
bad.why: It requires a kindness being repaid with harm; paying back harm with harm is a different idiom.

bad.s: 朋友送了我礼物，我{恩将仇报}，请他吃了顿饭。
bad.en: (meant: a friend gave me a gift, so I returned the favour with a meal)
bad.why: It means repaying kindness with harm; here a favour is being kindly returned.

mean: courtesy calls for courtesy in return

story.text: The phrase comes from the Book of Rites, which says that propriety values reciprocity: to give and receive nothing in return is not proper, and to receive and give nothing in return is not proper either.

use.how: Often a comment on its own or after 这叫/讲究: 这叫礼尚往来. Said about returning gifts, visits or favours; also used jokingly for paying back a jab.

near.diff: 投桃报李 is repaying one specific kindness gratefully; 礼尚往来 is the general custom of give and take, and can be used ironically.

cue: Last week your neighbour brought you homemade dumplings, so today you bring them a box of pastries. What custom are you following?

ctx.s: 你上次请我吃饭，这次我请你，这叫{礼尚往来}。
ctx.en: You treated me to dinner last time, so this time it's on me. That's give and take.

ctx.s: 邻居送来饺子，我们也回送了一盒点心，{礼尚往来}嘛。
ctx.en: The neighbours brought dumplings, so we sent back a box of pastries; one good turn deserves another.

ctx.s: 中国人讲究{礼尚往来}，收了别人的礼物，一般要找机会回礼。
ctx.en: Chinese people set store by reciprocity: if you receive a gift, you usually find a chance to give one back.

ctx.s: “你怎么又给我带茶叶了？”“你上次送我的书我很喜欢，{礼尚往来}。”
ctx.en: "You've brought me tea again?" "I loved the book you gave me last time. Fair's fair."

ctx.s: 两家公司每年互相派人参观学习，{礼尚往来}，关系越来越好。
ctx.en: Every year the two companies send staff to visit and learn from each other, and with this give and take their relationship keeps improving.

ctx.s: 他在会上挖苦了我一句，下次开会我也{礼尚往来}，回敬了他一句。
ctx.en: He took a dig at me in the meeting, so at the next one I returned the courtesy with a dig of my own.

bad.s: 他每年都送我生日礼物，我却从来不回礼，真是{礼尚往来}。
bad.en: (meant: he gives me presents but I never give any back)
bad.why: It means returning courtesy; never giving anything back is exactly the opposite of it.

bad.s: 老板，请您{礼尚往来}地批准我的假期。
bad.en: (meant: boss, please kindly approve my leave)
bad.why: It describes an exchange between two sides, not politeness in a request; it cannot mean 'kindly'.

mean: eyes brimming with tears of emotion
lit: hot tears filling the eye sockets

use.how: A predicate, often after 感动得/激动得: 感动得热泪盈眶. Tears welling up from being deeply moved, proud or overjoyed, not from pain.

near.diff: 泪流满面 is a face streaming with tears from any cause; 热泪盈眶 is tears welling in the eyes, usually from being moved.

cue: At your graduation your grandmother watches you walk across the stage, and her eyes fill with tears of pride. How does she look?

ctx.s: 看到女儿走上领奖台，妈妈{热泪盈眶}。
ctx.en: Seeing her daughter step onto the podium, the mother's eyes filled with tears.

ctx.s: 这部电影的结尾让很多观众{热泪盈眶}。
ctx.en: The ending of this film brought tears to many viewers' eyes.

ctx.s: “你怎么哭了？”“没什么，听到这首歌，突然就{热泪盈眶}了。”
ctx.en: "Why are you crying?" "It's nothing, I heard this song and my eyes just suddenly welled up."

ctx.s: 时隔多年回到故乡，老人站在老房子前{热泪盈眶}，却强忍着没让眼泪掉下来。
ctx.en: Back in his hometown after many years, the old man stood in front of his old house, eyes brimming, but held the tears back.

ctx.s: 收到全班同学写的感谢信，即将退休的老师感动得{热泪盈眶}。
ctx.en: Receiving a thank-you letter from the whole class, the teacher about to retire was moved to tears.

ctx.s: 终场哨声响起，坚持了四年的队员们{热泪盈眶}，紧紧抱在一起。
ctx.en: When the final whistle blew, the players who had stuck it out for four years hugged each other, tears welling in their eyes.

bad.s: 他摔断了腿，疼得{热泪盈眶}。
bad.en: (meant: he broke his leg and the pain made him cry)
bad.why: It is tears of being moved or proud, never tears caused by physical pain.

bad.s: 孩子丢了玩具，在地上{热泪盈眶}地大哭大闹。
bad.en: (meant: the child lost a toy and threw a crying tantrum on the floor)
bad.why: It describes quiet tears welling up from deep emotion, not loud crying in a tantrum.

mean: to kick someone when they are down
lit: when someone falls into a well, to drop stones on them

story.text: In his epitaph for his friend Liu Zongyuan, the Tang writer Han Yu criticised false friends: in good times they swear lifelong loyalty, but when a friend falls into a pit they do not reach down to pull him out; instead they push him further in and throw stones down on him.

use.how: A predicate, often 对某人落井下石 or 别落井下石. Condemns attacking or harming someone who is already in trouble.

near.diff: 趁火打劫 is grabbing gain from someone's crisis; 落井下石 is adding to the harm of someone already down.

cue: A colleague has just been demoted after a mistake, and another colleague goes to the boss to list all his old errors too. What is she doing?

ctx.s: 他已经很难过了，你别再{落井下石}了。
ctx.en: He's upset enough already; don't kick him while he's down.

ctx.s: 真正的朋友会在你困难时帮你，而不是{落井下石}。
ctx.en: A true friend helps you when you're struggling instead of piling on.

ctx.s: “他被辞退了，我们要不要也去告他一状？”“人家已经这样了，何必{落井下石}？”
ctx.en: "He's been fired. Should we file a complaint against him too?" "He's already in this state; why kick him when he's down?"

ctx.s: 公司出事以后，以前的合作伙伴纷纷{落井下石}，到处说他的坏话。
ctx.en: After his company got into trouble, his former partners one after another turned on him, badmouthing him everywhere.

ctx.s: 那位演员道歉以后，网上还有人{落井下石}，翻出他的旧事继续攻击。
ctx.en: After the actor apologised, people online still piled on, digging up his past to keep attacking him.

ctx.s: 这位球员受伤离场，对方球迷却在看台上起哄，这种{落井下石}的做法让人不齿。
ctx.en: The player was carried off injured, yet the opposing fans jeered from the stands; kicking someone when they're down like that is contemptible.

bad.s: 朋友生病住院，我{落井下石}，每天去医院照顾他。
bad.en: (meant: when my friend was in hospital I helped by visiting every day)
bad.why: It means harming someone in trouble; helping them in their trouble is the exact opposite.

bad.s: 我们公司{落井下石}，终于把产品卖到了国外。
bad.en: (meant: our company finally broke into foreign markets)
bad.why: It condemns attacking someone who has fallen; it has nothing to do with success or progress.

mean: to profit from someone else's crisis
lit: to loot a house while it is on fire

story.text: It is the fifth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, the traditional collection of tricks of war: when the enemy is struck by disaster or thrown into disorder, take that moment to attack and seize what you want.

use.how: A predicate or attributive: 这是趁火打劫, 趁火打劫的行为. Condemns using a disaster or someone's emergency to grab money or advantage.

near.diff: 落井下石 is harming someone already in trouble; 趁火打劫 is taking advantage of the trouble to gain something for oneself.

cue: During a flood, a shop next to the shelter triples the price of bottled water. What is it doing?

ctx.s: 台风来了，有的商店却把矿泉水涨价三倍，这不是{趁火打劫}吗？
ctx.en: With a typhoon coming, some shops tripled the price of bottled water. Isn't that exploiting the disaster?

ctx.s: “车坏在高速上，拖车要价两千。”“这明摆着是{趁火打劫}。”
ctx.en: "My car broke down on the motorway and the tow truck wants two thousand." "That's blatantly taking advantage of you."

ctx.s: 他家着急卖房子还债，买家拼命压价，简直是{趁火打劫}。
ctx.en: His family had to sell the house fast to pay debts, and the buyer kept forcing the price down. That's profiting from their crisis.

ctx.s: 疫情期间高价倒卖口罩，这种{趁火打劫}的行为必须严查。
ctx.en: Reselling masks at inflated prices during the epidemic is profiteering from a crisis and must be strictly investigated.

ctx.s: 公司陷入危机时，竞争对手{趁火打劫}，高薪挖走了他们的核心技术人员。
ctx.en: While the company was in crisis, a rival took advantage and poached its key engineers with high salaries.

ctx.s: 地震后，几个小偷{趁火打劫}，溜进没人看守的商店偷东西。
ctx.en: After the earthquake, a few thieves took advantage of the chaos and slipped into unguarded shops to steal.

bad.s: 消防员{趁火打劫}，冲进大楼救出了三个孩子。
bad.en: (meant: the firefighter rushed into the fire and rescued three children)
bad.why: It condemns profiting from a crisis; the fire image does not make it fit a rescue.

bad.s: 他考试没考好，同学们却{趁火打劫}，一直嘲笑他。
bad.en: (meant: he failed the exam and classmates kept mocking him)
bad.why: It needs someone grabbing a gain from the crisis; mocking a person who is down gains nothing.

lit: centres hooked together, corners vying with each other

story.text: The Tang poet Du Mu, describing the vast Epang Palace of the Qin, wrote that its buildings each followed the lie of the land, their centres hooking together and their roof corners contending like rivals. The phrase was first about architecture and later came to mean people plotting against each other.

use.how: A predicate or noun, often 互相勾心斗角 or 厌倦了勾心斗角. Said of people in one group, like colleagues or relatives, secretly plotting against each other.

near.diff: 明争暗斗 is rivalry both open and hidden; 勾心斗角 stresses the calculated, behind-the-scenes scheming.

cue: In an office, colleagues smile at each other but secretly plot to undermine one another for promotion. What is going on there?

ctx.s: 我不喜欢那家公司，同事之间总是{勾心斗角}。
ctx.en: I don't like that company; the colleagues are always scheming against each other.

ctx.s: 这部宫廷剧讲的是后宫妃子们{勾心斗角}的故事。
ctx.en: This palace drama is about the concubines of the imperial harem plotting against one another.

ctx.s: “你为什么辞职？”“我只想好好做事，不想每天跟人{勾心斗角}。”
ctx.en: "Why did you quit?" "I just want to do my job properly, not scheme against people every day."

ctx.s: 老人去世以后，几个子女为了遗产{勾心斗角}，亲情越来越淡。
ctx.en: After the old man died, his children schemed against each other over the inheritance, and the family bond faded.

ctx.s: 小团队人少事多，大家没时间{勾心斗角}，反而合作得很愉快。
ctx.en: In a small team with lots to do, nobody has time for intrigue, so people actually work together happily.

ctx.s: 他在这个圈子里待了几十年，早就厌倦了那些{勾心斗角}。
ctx.en: He's been in this circle for decades and has long since grown tired of all the intrigue.

bad.s: 两个队在决赛中{勾心斗角}，踢得非常精彩。
bad.en: (meant: the two teams battled hard in a thrilling final)
bad.why: It condemns secret scheming among insiders, not open, fair competition that one praises.

bad.s: 为了解出这道数学题，他{勾心斗角}了一个晚上。
bad.en: (meant: he racked his brains all evening over this maths problem)
bad.why: It means plotting against other people, not thinking hard about a problem on one's own.

mean: to meet point with point in sharp opposition

use.how: A predicate or adverbial: 双方针锋相对, 观点针锋相对, 针锋相对地反驳. Two sides directly opposing each other in argument, views or tactics.

near.diff: 以牙还牙 is paying back harm with the same harm; 针锋相对 is sharp, point-for-point opposition, usually in argument.

cue: In a meeting, every time one manager makes a point, the other immediately rebuts it point by point and neither gives ground. How are they arguing?

ctx.s: 会上两个部门的经理{针锋相对}，谁也不让谁。
ctx.en: At the meeting the two department managers went head to head, neither giving an inch.

ctx.s: 辩论赛上，正方和反方{针锋相对}，场面十分激烈。
ctx.en: In the debate the two sides clashed point for point, and it got very heated.

ctx.s: 对于房价问题，两位专家的观点{针锋相对}。
ctx.en: On the question of house prices, the two experts' views are diametrically opposed.

ctx.s: 采访中，记者的问题很尖锐，他的回答也{针锋相对}，毫不退让。
ctx.en: In the interview the journalist's questions were sharp, and his answers met them head on without backing down.

ctx.s: “他说我们的方案太贵，你怎么回应的？”“我{针锋相对}地列出了他们方案的隐藏成本。”
ctx.en: "He said our plan was too expensive; how did you respond?" "I countered directly by listing the hidden costs of their plan."

ctx.s: 对方加强了防守，我们也{针锋相对}，换上了两名进攻球员。
ctx.en: They tightened their defence, so we countered directly by bringing on two attacking players.

bad.s: 两个老朋友见面后{针锋相对}，聊得非常开心。
bad.en: (meant: the two old friends met face to face and had a lovely chat)
bad.why: It means sharp opposition, not sitting face to face for a friendly talk.

bad.s: 我和女朋友{针锋相对}，一起看了一场电影。
bad.en: (meant: my girlfriend and I sat together and watched a film)
bad.why: It describes two sides clashing in argument; it cannot mean being together or side by side.

use.how: A predicate, often with 要/先/带头: 父母要以身作则. Said of parents, teachers or leaders who do first what they ask of those under them.

near.diff: 身体力行 is personally practising what one advocates; 以身作则 is doing it so as to set the standard for others.

cue: A coach who wants the players on time always arrives first and leaves last, so the team follows. What is the coach doing?

ctx.s: 想让孩子少玩手机，父母先要{以身作则}。
ctx.en: If you want your kids on their phones less, you as parents have to set the example first.

ctx.s: 一个好领导不光会讲道理，更要{以身作则}。
ctx.en: A good leader doesn't just talk; above all they lead by example.

ctx.s: 队长在训练中{以身作则}，每次都跑在最前面。
ctx.en: The captain leads by example in training, always running at the front.

ctx.s: “你自己都不遵守规定，凭什么要求我们？”“好，从今天起我{以身作则}。”
ctx.en: "You don't follow the rules yourself, so what right do you have to demand it of us?" "Fine, from today I'll set the example."

ctx.s: 经理要求大家节约用纸，他自己先{以身作则}，所有文件都双面打印。
ctx.en: The manager asked everyone to save paper and set the example himself by printing every document double-sided.

ctx.s: 校长每天第一个到学校，{以身作则}，老师们也不好意思迟到了。
ctx.en: The principal is the first to arrive at school every day, setting an example, so the teachers are too embarrassed to be late.

bad.s: 他总是迟到，经常{以身作则}。
bad.en: (meant: he is always late and sets a bad example)
bad.why: It is praise for setting a good example; it cannot describe setting a bad one.

bad.s: 今天我{以身作则}，自己做了一顿晚饭吃。
bad.en: (meant: today I did it myself and cooked my own dinner)
bad.why: It means setting an example for others to follow; cooking for yourself has no one being led.

lit: wholly for the public, with nothing for oneself

use.how: A predicate or attributive praising someone who puts fairness and the common good above personal interest: 他办事大公无私. Often negated ironically: 他可不是大公无私.

near.diff: 铁面无私 is stern impartiality that bends for no one; 大公无私 stresses putting the common good above one's own interest.

cue: The village head shares out relief money after a flood, gives the most to the poorest families and takes nothing for his own household. What is he like?

ctx.s: 他处理问题{大公无私}，大家都很信任他。
ctx.en: He handles matters selflessly and fairly, so everyone trusts him.

ctx.s: “让他管这笔钱，你放心吗？”“放心，他这个人{大公无私}，一分钱也不会往自己口袋里装。”
ctx.en: "Are you comfortable with him managing this money?" "Yes, he puts the common good first; he won't pocket a single cent."

ctx.s: 评比时，班长把奖励给了表现更好的同学，没有给自己的好朋友，真是{大公无私}。
ctx.en: In the class awards, the monitor gave the prize to the classmate who did better, not to her best friend. Truly impartial.

ctx.s: 这位老会计{大公无私}，单位分房时主动把名额让给了更困难的同事。
ctx.en: The old accountant is selfless: when the work unit allocated flats, he gave up his place to a colleague in greater need.

ctx.s: 村里分配补助时，村长{大公无私}，先照顾最困难的人家，自己家一分不要。
ctx.en: When the village shared out aid, the village head acted selflessly, looking after the neediest families first and taking nothing for his own.

ctx.s: 别把他想得那么{大公无私}，他推荐的人其实都是他的老同学。
ctx.en: Don't think he's so selfless; the people he recommends are actually all his old classmates.

bad.s: 他{大公无私}地把所有零食都给了女朋友。
bad.en: (meant: he generously gave all his snacks to his girlfriend)
bad.why: It praises putting the common good and fairness above private ties; favouring one's girlfriend is not it.

bad.s: 这家餐厅的菜很{大公无私}，分量特别足。
bad.en: (meant: this restaurant is generous, the portions are big)
bad.why: It describes a person's integrity in public matters, not generosity of food or things.
